title: The Word was made flesh (John 1:9–14)
hook: and dwelt among us; Catholics once genuflected at this line in nearly every Mass

segments.voice: Yesterday, logos: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God. Your line was the word was God.

Et Verbum caro factum est. In the old Latin Mass, the Mass is over, or nearly. The priest has given the blessing, and now he walks to the left side of the altar and reads in Latin from the first chapter of John, a reading called the Last Gospel. The people are standing. They know where this is going. They are waiting for one line. When it comes, priest and people go down on one knee together. Then they stand again.
screen: `THE OLD LATIN MASS.` → `THE PRIEST READS JOHN IN LATIN.` → `EVERYONE KNEELS AT ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Before the line, John tells a hard truth. The true light came into the world, and the world, made by him, didn't know him. "He came unto his own, and his own received him not." But some did, and to them he gave power to become children of God. Then the line: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." In Latin, Et Verbum caro factum est. That's where they knelt. Yesterday the Word was with God before creation. Today the same Word has skin, and hunger, and a mother. Flesh is a blunt word: not a body, or a human nature, but the soft, mortal, breakable stuff we're made of. Then dwelt. The Greek verb literally means pitched his tent, and readers hear in it the tabernacle in the desert, the tent where God's glory came to dwell among Israel. John goes on: "and we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." The Church calls this the Incarnation, from the Latin for in the flesh. The genuflection at the Last Gospel is mostly gone now, since that reading left the ordinary form of the Mass after the Second Vatican Council. But the gesture lives on. In the Creed, at the words about the Son becoming man, Catholics bow; on Christmas and the feast of the Annunciation, they kneel at those words instead. Those who pray the Angelus traditionally kneel at this very line. The body bends at the moment God is said to take a body.
screen: `HIS OWN RECEIVED HIM NOT.` · `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.` · `DWELT: HE PITCHED HIS TENT.` · `STILL WE BOW AT THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Stand or sit tall, and say the words slowly: and the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. At made flesh, bow your head, or bend at the waist, or kneel if that's your way, and hold it for a breath before coming back up. If you pray, let the bow be your prayer; if you don't, just notice what it is to bend your body at a thought.
Eskenosen. John's word for dwelt, pitched his tent: the eternal Word who took on a human body and lived among us. Today's word.
Your line: and dwelt among us. The Word chose an address of his own. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics bow at the words of the Incarnation in the Creed and genuflect there on Christmas and the Annunciation; those who pray the Angelus traditionally kneel at "and the Word was made flesh".

fork.setup: you're John, writing the line at the heart of your opening. you want to say God's Word became human. which word do you choose?
options: he took on a human nature.
fork.reveal: John chose flesh, the blunt word for soft, mortal stuff, and dwelt, literally pitched his tent among us.

original.note: Greek: he pitched his tent, dwelt (John 1:14); from skēnē, a tent, the word used for the tabernacle.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Word was made flesh is a poetic way of saying Christmas.
what it means: the eternal Word, who is God, took on real human flesh and lived among people.
what a scholar hears: eskēnōsen, he tented, echoes the desert tabernacle and God's glory dwelling with Israel; then John says: we saw his glory.

chat.says: Why did people kneel at one line at the end of the old Latin Mass?
options: It's the line where the Word was made flesh; the body bends where God takes a body.
It was where the priest named the pope and bishop, so people knelt out of respect.
It marked the end of Mass; kneeling was how people said goodbye to the altar.
chat.meaning: At the Last Gospel, priest and people knelt at 'and the Word was made flesh': the Incarnation, God taking a body.

notes: The voice splits the John 1:14 quotation in two ('And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.' then 'and we saw his glory...'); the source records the full verse. Confirm the Douay parentheses.
Hook softened in review from 'every Mass' to 'nearly every Mass' (the Last Gospel was omitted at some Masses, e.g. when a proper Last Gospel or none applied). Confirm.
GIRM 137: bow at the Incarnation in the Creed, genuflect on Christmas and the Annunciation. Confirm.
Last Gospel dropped from the ordinary Mass in 1964 (Inter Oecumenici). Stated as 'in the 1960s'. Confirm.
Angelus custom of kneeling at 'And the Word was made flesh': confirm phrasing ('many kneel').
'A hundred years ago' and the whole congregation genuflecting: described as the general custom; confirm.
